newsitem.title: USA: William Daley - the "other" Chicago Daley.
newsitem.headline: William Daley - the "other" Chicago Daley.

text.p: William Daley, nominated as commerce secretary on Friday, won the respect of the White House by organising the effort that pushed the North American Free Trade Agreement through Congress.
Unlike his brother, Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, or his father, the late Mayor Richard J. Daley, the 48-year-old Daley is a banker and lawyer who largely operates behind the scenes.

He was in the spotlight, however, as co-chairman of last summer's Democratic National Convention. The party convention in Chicago launched President Bill Clinton on his winning campaign for a second term, and Clinton nominated Daley for the Cabinet post on Friday.

Daley became involved in Clinton's first presidential campaign early, chairing it in Illinois. He was credited with playing a key role in helping the then Arkansas governor capture Illinois and several other important states.
Four years ago, he was widely mentioned as a likely candidate for the transportation post that ultimately went to Federico Pena.

Daley was the chief White House lobbyist for the Free Trade Agreement and was credited with organising the arm-twisting campaign that got it through Congress despite the resistance of many fellow Democrats.

In Chicago William Daley has long been considered by City Hall insiders as "co-mayor," a bald and brainy strategist involved in almost every detail of what happens in his older brother Richard's office.
In September 1990, he became president of Amalgamated Bank of Chicago, a bank founded by the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America in 1922 and one that has had strong trade union ties ever since.

He stepped down from that post in 1993 to concentrate on his law career with the firm of Mayer, Brown and Platt. In the summer of 1992, Daley was elected to the board of Wheelabrator Technologies Inc., a subsidiary of Waste Management Inc.
He serves on the boards of a wide range of civic and business organisations, including the Oak Brook, Ill., Bank, the ChicagoLand Chamber of Commerce and the America's Leaders Fund.
He is on the advisory boards of the J.L. Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University, Catholic Charities of Chicago and the Federal National Mortgage Association.
He is the youngest of four sons of the late mayor -- the other brothers being Michael and John. He has three sisters, Mary, Pat and Ellen.
Daley attended Nativity of Our Lord grammar school and St. Ignatius prep school in Chicago.
He was graduated from Loyola University in Chicago in 1970 and has a law degree from Chicago's John Marshall Law School. Daley and his wife, Loretta, have three children.
